title: Castor and Pollux Share Immortality
text:
Castor and Polydeuces (Pollux to the Romans) were twin brothers who never left each other's side. But they did not share the same father. Polydeuces was the son of Zeus and immortal. Castor was the son of a mortal man and would one day die.

In a quarrel with two other brothers, Idas and Lynceus, Castor was killed by Idas's spear. Polydeuces chased down the killers; Zeus struck Idas with a thunderbolt. Then Polydeuces returned to find his brother dying.

Weeping, he called out to his father Zeus and asked to die with Castor. Without his brother, he said, life had no honor.

Zeus came to him and gave him a choice. He could live forever on Olympus among the gods, untouched by age or death. Or he could share his immortality with his brother: half their days they would spend beneath the earth, and half in the golden homes of heaven.

Polydeuces did not hesitate. He chose to share. Zeus opened the eyes of Castor, who had been dead, and freed his voice. From then on, according to Pindar, the two brothers alternate between the world below and the home of the gods, never apart.
lesson: Loyalty between siblings can mean choosing to share losses as well as gifts. What is given up for a brother or sister is rarely regretted.
